description: The hand-verified expected result for the negative Opengrep SARIF fixture whose defect is structural: an element of runs[0].results[] that is not the shape the adapter requires, while the enclosing document stays well-formed JSON. Every value was derived by reading the fixture and the authored contracts in harness/lib/normalize/, never by running the adapter and recording what it printed. Where this file and harness/lib/normalize/adapters/sarif.py disagree, the disagreement is the finding: diagnose it rather than overwriting this file to match. One thing a reader arriving with an expectation of a single rejection must see first: the fixture as committed carries TWO malformed elements, not one -- /runs/0/results/1 is a bare string where a result object belongs, and /runs/0/results/3 is an object whose message is a bare string where a message object belongs. Both are the same class, malformed_record, reached by two different steps of the adapter's fixed classification order, so the counts below are 4 == 2 + 2 with rejections_by_class {malformed_record: 2}. That is what the fixture yields; the fixture was not edited to bring the number to one, because trimming an input to make a count fit is the one move that would make every number here unreproducible.

fixture.derivation: A negative fixture is derived from the captured one rather than being an excerpt of it, so the provenance is stated as a derivation. Two of the four results are unmodified captured output: /runs/0/results/0 is structurally identical to harness/artifacts/raw/opengrep.sarif results[0] and to the positive fixture's results[0], and /runs/0/results/2 is structurally identical to that artifact's results[432] and the positive fixture's results[1] -- each confirmed by its own matchBasedId/v1 fingerprint as well as by whole-record comparison. The other two are the synthesized defective records. /runs/0/results/1 is the ruleId string of results[0] standing alone as an array element, so the element is a JSON string where a result object belongs. /runs/0/results/3 is a complete, realistic result -- a real location in the pinned tree, a real rule, a real snippet -- whose message is the rule's description text placed directly under the message key instead of under message.text, so the element is an object with a structurally wrong message.
fixture.captured_provenance: Neither synthesized record appears in harness/artifacts/raw/opengrep.sarif nor in oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/fixtures/opengrep.sarif. The raw artifact carries no record naming OneForOneBlockPusher.java at all, and /runs/0/results/3 matches nothing in either file even when its message is disregarded entirely, which is what makes both records demonstrably this fixture's own additions rather than something the tool emitted. The recorded sha256 above is what makes a later edit to the fixture visible: these values are re-derived when the fixture changes, never adjusted to keep a test green.
fixture.not_records: Three parts of this document are finding-shaped without being finding records, and none of them is counted. /runs/0/invocations/0 carries only executionSuccessful true -- there are no toolExecutionNotifications in this fixture. The two entries under /runs/0/tool/driver/rules are rule metadata, reached by the adapter to resolve a level and a weakness identifier, never walked as records. And the bare string at /runs/0/results/1 is a record: it is an element of the count-unit array, so it counts as one raw record even though nothing can be read out of it. A reading that counted rule objects, or that skipped the string because it looked like metadata, would arrive at a number other than four and fail the reconciliation identity for a reason that has nothing to do with the adapter.

routing.detected_by: normalize.shape.is_sarif -- a version of "2.1.0" together with a runs array; those two together are the whole test
routing.routing_decision: normalize.shape.route("opengrep", doc) returns tool "opengrep", shape "sarif", adapter "sarif", scanner_class "sast"
routing.not_a_shape_failure: No normalize.shape.UnknownArtifactShape is expected here, and a test asserting one against this fixture would be asserting the wrong thing. The enclosing document is valid SARIF 2.1.0 and routes cleanly; two records inside it are structurally defective, and the adapter rejects those two while still emitting the others. The fixtures that own shape-detection failure are near-sarif-version-only.json, near-sarif-runs-only.json and unknown-shape.json.
routing.negative_routing_test: The mandated negative routing assertion -- that a native artifact must not route to the SARIF adapter -- belongs to test_shape_routing_negative.py and does not use this fixture.

field_order_authority: harness/lib/normalize/emit.py, the FIELDS constant. Every row below carries all twelve keys in that order, present-with-null rather than omitted.
absence_convention: Absence is JSON null here and in findings.json, and an empty field in findings.csv. tool, scanner_class, rule_id, message, severity_norm, path and in_scope are never absent -- exactly emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS.

allowlist.note: in_scope is decided by that file alone. The globs are not copied here: the allowlist is the single authority and stays byte-exact. The glob each row matched is recorded per row under row_derivations.

resolution_context.root_independence: Both surviving uris are already root-relative, and the recorded path base for opengrep is the scan root itself, so joining onto the base and relativizing back to the root returns each uri unchanged. These rows therefore hold for whatever absolute scan root the adapter is given, and no absolute path appears anywhere in this file. Neither rejected record depends on a root either, for a reason that has nothing to do with paths: both are classified on their shape, before any path is looked at.
resolution_context.path_base_source: harness/artifacts/logs/runner-metadata.json, the opengrep entry's path_base -- read as input, never assumed
resolution_context.uri_base_id_walk_consequence: With no run.originalUriBaseIds the SARIF 2.1.0 section 3.4.4 procedure cannot complete -- the documented producer gap -- and that outcome is eligible for the metadata-backed fallback, so each resolvable path resolves against the runner-recorded base rather than being rejected. Neither defective record reaches this walk: the string element is rejected at step 1 and the wrong-message record at step 3, both before step 4 looks at a path.
resolution_context.severity_source: Neither surviving result states a level, and neither rule carries properties.severity or properties.problem.severity, so each severity_native is the level its own rule states under defaultConfiguration.level and each severity_norm comes from the SARIF level table: error High, warning Medium, note Low, none Info.
resolution_context.package_coordinate: null on every row. A SARIF result names a code location rather than a package, and this shape supplies no coordinate to carry.

rejection_boundary.statement: A malformed record is a record whose container is not the shape its adapter requires, so nothing can be read out of it with any confidence. It is rejected and counted under malformed_record, never coerced into a row and never dropped. paths.py states the class in one line: "the record is not the shape its adapter requires".
rejection_boundary.why_it_can_only_be_a_rejection: Seven of the twelve fields are never absent from a row -- tool, scanner_class, rule_id, message, severity_norm, path and in_scope. A record that is not an object supplies none of them, and a record whose message is not an object supplies no message text; there is no valid row representation of either, and the alternatives are worse than a rejection. Dropping the record silently would break the identity raw == rows + rejections. Guessing values would put content in the dataset that the artifact does not contain.
rejection_boundary.document_versus_record_scope: This is the property that makes malformed_record a per-record class at all, and it is worth stating because the two failures look alike in a summary and behave nothing alike. A syntactically broken DOCUMENT -- a truncated write, an unbalanced brace -- fails json.load upstream in cli.py, before any record is reached. Nothing is walked, so there is no per-record rejection, no partial parse, no counter and no reconciliation for that artifact: the outcome is a parse failure over the whole file. This fixture is deliberately not that case. Its bytes are well-formed JSON and json.load succeeds, so the walk reaches every one of the four elements and the defect is confined to two of them. No json.load failure is expected here, and a test that asserted one would be exercising the wrong boundary.
rejection_boundary.malformed_element_is_inside_the_count_un: Both defective elements sit inside runs[0].results[], the count unit reconcile.count_records walks, so both are raw records and the identity has something to prove. Had either been placed outside that array -- a stray key on the run, an extra member beside results -- reconcile would not count it, the arithmetic would still balance, and the fixture would demonstrate nothing about how a defective record is handled.
rejection_boundary.unchecked_access_would_raise: The bare string at /runs/0/results/1 is the shape a truncated or mis-serialised producer write actually takes, and it is the shape that defeats unchecked dict-style access: in Python, result["ruleId"] on a str raises TypeError and result.get(...) raises AttributeError. Correct handling turns that raise into a counted rejection rather than a crash, and the crash is the expensive failure -- it would abandon the artifact at element 1 and lose elements 2 and 3 with it. This fixture proves the difference by construction: a surviving row and a second rejection both come from positions after the string, so a run that stopped at element 1 cannot produce these counts. The adapter's own contract is what makes this structural rather than defensive: _adapt_result returns exactly one of a row or a rejection for every element it is handed, and it narrows the type once, at the top, instead of catching broadly further down.
rejection_boundary.two_records_one_class: Both rejections here are malformed_record, and they are not a duplication. The class is one; the routes to it are two, and they are two different steps of the adapter's fixed classification order. Step 1 rejects an element that is not an object -- nothing about it can be read. Step 3 rejects an object whose message is present but is not an object -- everything before the message was readable, which is why this record's rule identifier appears in the rule counter while contributing no row. Covering both routes in one fixture is what makes the class's coverage complete rather than nominal.

not_a_rejection.case: a message object that carries no text, or a text that is empty or whitespace only
not_a_rejection.expected: a missing_message rejection, a different class entirely
not_a_rejection.evidence: The adapter keeps the two apart deliberately: a producer that omits message text is a different fact from an artifact that is not shaped like SARIF, and a reader of tool-status.md acts differently on each. /runs/0/results/3 is the malformed side of that boundary -- its message is present and non-empty, and wrong only in its container.

not_a_rejection.case: a run that is not an object, or a run carrying no results array
not_a_rejection.expected: no record at all -- counted under runs_skipped_non_mapping or runs_without_results_array, contributing neither a row nor a rejection
not_a_rejection.evidence: reconcile.count_records treats both the same way, contributing zero, so the two traversals agree without either raising. Both counters are 0 here: this document's single run is an object and carries a results array.

not_a_rejection.case: a region that is not an object, a locations value that is not an array, or a member of the location chain that is not an object
not_a_rejection.expected: also malformed_record, but reached at step 4 through the location chain rather than at step 1 or step 3
not_a_rejection.evidence: Named so the class's full surface is visible rather than implied. Every location chain in this fixture's two surviving records is well formed, and the wrong-message record is rejected before its own well-formed chain is ever inspected.

rejection_boundary.no_guessed_field: Neither rejected record is given a rule identifier it did not carry, a message assembled from its rule's description, or a path taken from its location. Each rejection carries only what identifies the record in the artifact -- run index, result index, and for the second one the rule identifier it did resolve -- so the record can be found again without any of its content being invented.

counts.raw_count_unit: one element of runs[].results[] -- the unit normalize.reconcile.count_records walks independently of row construction
counts.raw_count_authority: normalize.reconcile.count_records("opengrep", doc), whose SARIF traversal sums the length of each run's results array and builds no row, resolves no path and maps no severity. It is the independent half of the identity: a count taken from the traversal that builds the rows would satisfy the assertion while testing nothing.
counts.raw_count_includes_the_malformed_element: Yes, and this is the number to check first. Four is two surviving records plus the bare string at index 1 plus the wrong-message object at index 3. The traversal reads only the container it needs in order to walk -- runs, then results, then the length -- so an element it can make no sense of still counts as one record.

four_reported_counters.authority: AAP 0.5.4 -- the four counts reported per tool
four_reported_counters.note: Named here rather than restated with their values. The counters block below is the single measurement, and a number carried twice inside one document is a number that can drift; counters_note gives the reason each of the four is zero.

counts.parse_status_authority: harness/lib/normalize/cli.py, PARSE_STATUS_PARTIAL = "partial", assigned as partial where there are rejections and clean where there are none. Partial is right precisely because the adapter did not abandon the artifact: every parsable record was emitted and each rejected record is counted under its class, with its parser reason retained. This is deliberately not normalize.reconcile's STATUS_PASS / STATUS_FAIL / STATUS_NOT_APPLICABLE vocabulary, which describes an assertion's outcome rather than an artifact's parse. It is also not the failed status a shape mismatch earns: partial says the artifact was read and part of it could not be attributed, which is the whole point of this fixture.

counters_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/sarif.py, COUNTER_KEYS as returned by new_counters(): twenty authored keys, one path_kind_* per path kind and one severity_basis_* per severity basis, twenty-nine in total.
counters_note: Three things a reader must not "correct". First, rule_id_from_rule_id is 3 while the severity counters are 2, and the difference is one record rather than a miscount: the rule identifier is step 2 and the message is step 3, so /runs/0/results/3 resolves its ruleId and is counted for it, then is rejected before severity is ever resolved. Second, that same asymmetry does not extend to /runs/0/results/1: a bare string is rejected at step 1, so it reaches no counter at all -- which is why the rule counter is 3 and not 4. Third, the four counters AAP 0.5.4 has reported per tool are all 0 here. Every object element carries exactly one location, so multi_location_records is 0 -- and note that the multi-location count is taken after the message step, so the wrong-message record's locations array is never inspected either way. The one rule that names a weakness names exactly one, so multi_valued_cwe_records is 0; no rule string carries a CVE identifier, so multi_valued_cve_records is 0; and both emitted paths name a file inside the scanned tree, so non_filesystem_paths is 0. Neither rejected record contributes to any path_kind_* or severity_basis_* counter, because neither produced a row.

corroboration.note: The two surviving results are the same two captured results the positive sibling covers, in the same order -- this file's row 0 is that file's row 0 and this file's row 1 is that file's row 1 -- and all twenty-four field comparisons agree. Recorded after the fact rather than as the source of these values: each value here was derived from the fixture and the authored contracts, so a future disagreement between this file and the adapter is a finding to diagnose rather than a diff to apply. Neither rejected record has a counterpart to corroborate against: both are this fixture's own synthesized additions, they appear in no captured artifact, and they contribute no dataset row.

rows.message: This if statement will always have the same behavior and is therefore unnecessary.

User data flows into this manually-constructed SQL string. User data can be safely inserted into SQL strings using prepared statements or an object-relational mapper (ORM). Manually-constructed SQL strings is a possible indicator of SQL injection, which could let an attacker steal or manipulate data from the database. Instead, use prepared statements (`connection.PreparedStatement`) or a safe library.

rows_note: Both surviving rows are listed in full rather than referred to, so the partial-parse outcome is visible rather than inferred: this artifact produced rows AND rejections, and here are the rows. Two is also the minimum that makes the outcome unambiguous -- one row could be read as the adapter having stopped somewhere, whereas two rows straddling a rejection cannot.

row_derivations.rule_id_source: the result's own ruleId; no ruleIndex and no rule reference is present
row_derivations.severity_native_note: the result states no level, and its rule carries neither properties.severity nor properties.problem.severity, so all three field sources AAP 0.5.4 authorises for a SARIF record are silent; the absence is stated rather than filled from rule.defaultConfiguration.level, which AAP 0.5.4 does not carry as a field source
row_derivations.cwe_absent_reason: the rule carries no properties.cwe and its properties.tags array is empty, so no CWE token exists to collect -- and the identifier sources are those two rule properties only, never the rule's description or help text
row_derivations.anchor_note: The row that precedes both rejections, and the one a crash at element 1 would still have produced. It proves nothing about traversal on its own, which is why the second row matters. Its region is real at the pin: line 112 of that file is the `if (shouldClose) {` the snippet quotes.

row_derivations.rule_id_source: the result's own ruleId; no ruleIndex and no rule reference is present
row_derivations.severity_native_note: the result states no level, and its rule carries neither properties.severity nor properties.problem.severity, so all three field sources AAP 0.5.4 authorises for a SARIF record are silent; the absence is stated rather than filled from rule.defaultConfiguration.level, which AAP 0.5.4 does not carry as a field source

cwe_source.text: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

row_derivations.cwe_selection: One distinct identifier, so the ascending-numeric rule selects it without a comparison. The emitted value keeps the digits exactly as the tag wrote them under the canonical CWE- prefix, and nothing after the colon enters any field.
row_derivations.cve_absent_reason: The rule's four remaining tags are MEDIUM CONFIDENCE, OWASP-A01:2017 - Injection, OWASP-A03:2021 - Injection and security. None matches the CVE token pattern -- a four-digit year and a sequence of at least four digits after a CVE- prefix -- so no CVE identifier exists to select, and the OWASP tags' years are not read as one.
row_derivations.anchor_note: The row that carries the traversal proof: it comes from element 2, after the bare string at element 1, so a run that crashed on the string could not have produced it. Its region is real at the pin -- line 72 of DiskStore.scala is the interpolated string inside the SparkException.internalError call opened at line 71, the same anchor the Opengrep taint A/B uses -- and 72 is within the file's 380 lines.

rejections.locator_note: The pointer and the run_index / result_index pair name the same record. The pair is carried as well because normalize.adapters.sarif passes exactly run_index, result_index and rule_id into the rejection it builds, so a produced Rejection's record_identity and this expectation can be compared directly, without translating one coordinate system into the other.
rejections.reject_class_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, the REJECT_MALFORMED_RECORD constant -- a literal member of paths.REJECT_CLASSES, the closed set of ten, whose value is the string malformed_record. Written verbatim rather than paraphrased, and asserted against the module rather than by eye: a test that only counts rejections cannot tell one condition from another, so the class name is what carries the assertion.
rejections.classification_step: step 1 of the adapter's fixed classification order -- shape, rule identifier, message, path, start_line. The element is not a JSON object, so there is nothing to run steps 2 to 5 against and none of them is attempted.
rejections.element_value_note: The synthesized element is the rule identifier of the record before it, standing alone as an array member -- a plausible mis-serialisation rather than an arbitrary token. Its resemblance to a ruleId is deliberate and changes nothing: the adapter classifies on the element's JSON type, not on what its text looks like, so a string that happens to name a real rule is still a string where an object belongs.
rejections.expected_detail: the results element is a string, not an object, so no finding can be read from it
rejections.expected_detail_note: Retained verbatim, as AAP 0.5.4 requires of every rejection's parser reason. The detail is the sub-reason, and it is what distinguishes this record from the other malformed_record in the same artifact: the class alone would not say which of the two shapes was met. A test may assert the class exactly and the detail by its distinguishing substrings -- "is a string, not an object" -- rather than by full-string equality, since the detail names the element's own JSON type.
rejections.record_identity_note: Two keys and no more. rule_id is absent because step 2 never ran: the adapter supplies it only from a rule it actually resolved, and inventing one from the element's text would be the inference AAP 0.5.4 forbids. Enough to find the record in the artifact again, and never the record's own content.
rejections.why_not_a_row: A string carries no ruleId, no message, no location and no level. Six of the seven never-absent fields have no source in it, so no row can be formed at all -- this is the least ambiguous of all the rejection conditions.
rejections.contributes_no_counter: This record reaches no counter. It is not counted for its rule identifier, its severity, its path kind or its scope, because each of those counters is bumped at a step this record never reaches. That is what makes rule_id_from_rule_id 3 rather than 4.
rejections.contributes_no_severity_literal: The rejected record is never fed to the severity tally, so no native literal from it reaches severity-map.md. That document reports literals against the rows the dataset contains, and this record contributes none.

rejections.locator_note: The pointer and the run_index / result_index pair name the same record, and this is the last element of the array -- the position that makes the ordering visible: the walk reached it, which it could not have done had the string at index 1 stopped it.
rejections.reject_class_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, the REJECT_MALFORMED_RECORD constant -- the same literal member of paths.REJECT_CLASSES as the rejection above. One class, two routes.
rejections.classification_step: step 3 of the adapter's fixed classification order. Step 1 passes -- the element is a JSON object. Step 2 passes -- it carries a ruleId that resolves to /runs/0/tool/driver/rules/0. Step 3 fails, and fails structurally: the message key is present and non-empty but holds a string where SARIF 2.1.0 requires a message object, so the adapter classifies it malformed_record rather than missing_message. Steps 4 and 5 are never reached.
rejections.message_text_pointer_absent: There is no /runs/0/results/3/message/text to read. The text a well-formed record would carry sits directly under the message key instead, which is exactly why a consumer that reached for message.text with unchecked access would raise here rather than find an absence.
rejections.not_missing_message: This is the boundary the two classes share, and the fixture sits on the malformed side of it on purpose. missing_message covers a message object with no text, an empty text, a whitespace-only text and a text that is not a string; malformed_record covers a message that is not an object at all. The distinction is not cosmetic: one says the producer omitted content, the other says the artifact is not shaped the way the format requires, and tool-status.md is read differently for each. reject-sarif-missing-message.sarif owns the other side.
rejections.expected_detail: the result's message is a string, not an object
rejections.expected_detail_note: Retained verbatim. Distinguishing substrings for a test that prefers them to full-string equality: "message is a string" and "not an object".
rejections.record_identity_note: Three keys, one more than the rejection above, and the difference is evidence rather than inconsistency: this record's rule identifier was genuinely resolved at step 2 before step 3 rejected it, so the adapter has a real value to carry. Nothing here is guessed, and no location, snippet or message content is carried into the identity.
rejections.why_not_a_row: message is one of the seven never-absent fields. The record's other fields are all readable -- a rule, a real location, a real line -- and that is precisely the trap: emitting a row with everything except a message, or with the message key's string quietly accepted, would put a record in the dataset whose shape the artifact does not vouch for. Rejecting it and counting it keeps the defect visible.

location_never_emitted.note: Recorded to be explicit that this is not a path problem. The location is real at the pin -- line 90 of that file is the `if (returnCode != ReturnCode.SUCCESS) {` the snippet quotes, and 90 is within the file's 171 lines -- and it would have resolved and been in scope. It is stated here, outside the rows array, precisely because it must NOT appear as a row: a rejected record contributes none, and its resolvable path is the reason the fixture isolates the message container as the only thing wrong.

rejections.start_line_never_examined: Step 5 is never reached, so this record's region.startLine of 90 is never examined and non_integer_start_line is not in play. Worth stating because the value is a perfectly good line number, and a reader could otherwise expect it to surface somewhere.
rejections.contributes_no_severity_literal: Never fed to the severity tally. Its rule states level error under defaultConfiguration, and that literal reaches severity-map.md through the two emitted rows rather than through this record -- which is why severity_from_rule_default_configuration is 2 and not 3.

sarif_negative_set.this_fixture_is: the reject-sarif-* fixture for malformed_record, the last of the ten

fixtures.condition_named: a uriBaseId absent from originalUriBaseIds -- one of the bounded chain walk's terminal cases
a uriBaseId chain beyond the fixed depth
a chain terminating on a relative reference with no absolute ancestor

sarif_negative_set.outcome_ownership: Each of the other nine fixtures' expected outcome -- its rows, its rejection class and its counts -- is stated in its own expected file, not here. This file names them only to place itself in the set, and a number for any of them read off this list would be a number with no measurement behind it.
sarif_negative_set.coverage_observation: Of those seven, six are named by a fixture in this set. absent_path is named by none: the adapter reaches it through a result with no locations array, an empty one, a location with no physicalLocation, or a physicalLocation with no artifactLocation. Recorded as an observation about the set rather than resolved here, since adding a fixture is not this file's to do and a coverage gap nobody wrote down is a coverage gap nobody checks.

conditions_this_adapter_cannot_produce.why_unreachable_here: It is the outcome of resolving a bytecode class key against the source index and finding two or more distinct source files claiming it. A SARIF result names a source location outright -- a uri and a region -- so there is no class-to-source resolution to be ambiguous about. reject-joern-ambiguous-path.json owns it.

conditions_this_adapter_cannot_produce.produced_by: the dependency-oriented adapters -- trivy and dependency-check, and osv-scanner had it written an artifact
conditions_this_adapter_cannot_produce.why_unreachable_here: The SARIF shape supplies no package coordinate at all: package_coordinate is null on every row this adapter emits, by the field-source table rather than by accident. A field that is never formed cannot fail to form, so the condition has no route into this adapter. reject-trivy-no-package-coordinate.json and reject-dependency-check-no-package-coordinate.json own it.

Sections are a structure of a Trivy report -- Vulnerabilities, Secrets and Misconfigurations under one Results entry -- and a record's scanner_class is derived from which of them it was read from. SARIF has no equivalent: scanner_class is sast for every row this adapter emits, fixed per tool by the class table, so there is nothing to fail to attribute. reject-trivy-unattributable-section.json owns it.

sarif_negative_set.absence_reads_as_a_decision: Those three are named so their absence from the reject-sarif-* set is legible as a property of the SARIF shape rather than as three fixtures somebody forgot. Seven producible plus three unreachable is the closed set of ten in paths.REJECT_CLASSES, so the accounting is complete.

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: a document that is not well-formed JSON, failing json.load before any record is walked
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: the whole point of this fixture is the per-record class, which only exists because the document parses; rejection_boundary.document_versus_record_scope states the distinction
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.cover_with: nothing in this tree -- a parse failure over the whole file is cli.py's concern and produces no rows, no rejections and no reconciliation for that artifact

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: shape-detection failure -- an artifact matching neither SARIF nor a known native shape halting the run
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: this document is valid SARIF 2.1.0 and routes cleanly; its defect is two records, not its shape

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: the five other rejection conditions this adapter can reach -- absent_path, unresolvable_path, invalid_uri, missing_rule_id and non_integer_start_line
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: this fixture isolates one class, so every defective record here is defective in that one way; each other condition has its own fixture, and the two malformed elements differ in route rather than in class
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.cover_with: the sibling negative fixtures in this tree, listed under sarif_negative_set with the condition each names. Which outcome each of those asserts is stated in its own expected file, not here.

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: the two malformed_record routes this fixture does not take -- a locations value that is not an array, a location or physicalLocation or artifactLocation member that is not an object, and a region that is not an object
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: those are reached at step 4 through the location chain, and both defective records here are classified before step 4 runs
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.cover_with: a derived fixture whose location chain carries a non-object member, and one whose region is a string

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: the bounded uriBaseId chain walk and its terminal cases, including the metadata-backed fallback being refused where no explicit base is recorded
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: the two surviving records resolve through the fallback with the walk reporting the absent outcome, and neither defective record reaches a path at all

prohibitions_observed.no_secret_value: No field in this file carries a secret, a credential or a token. The fixture is Opengrep SAST output over source locations and contains none; the two rejections carry a run index, a result index and one rule identifier between them, and no record content beyond the JSON type that made each record defective.
prohibitions_observed.no_cross_tool_interpretation: One tool is named, opengrep, in each row's tool field and nowhere else does this file relate one tool's output to another's. The sibling fixtures and adapters referenced above are named to place this fixture in its set and to say which file owns which condition -- never to compare what any tool found or to explain why one tool reported something another did not.
prohibitions_observed.no_deduplication: Nothing here is merged. The two rejections are two records because the artifact carries two defective elements, and two identical results from one tool would likewise be two rows.
prohibitions_observed.no_judgement: Neither surviving row is characterised as real, important, a false positive or a duplicate, and neither rejected record is characterised as a tool defect. A rejection is a statement about what could be read out of a record, not about whether the finding was worth reporting.
